title: How websites store passwords
sources: OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet: 'Passwords should never be stored in plain text'; encryption is two-way, so attackers can retrieve plaintext from encrypted data; hashing is one-way, but an attacker can still guess candidates and compare hashes; a salt is a unique, random string added to each password; salting defeats precomputed rainbow-table/lookup attacks, and different salts give different hashes even for the same password; Argon2id is the first choice (min 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, parallelism 1); scrypt, bcrypt (legacy), PBKDF2 (FIPS) are alternatives. https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html

Example values: the password 'cat123', the hash strings and the user names are made-up illustrations, not real hashes. 'Slow on purpose' is a plain-language summary of OWASP's work-factor settings; the login compare flow is simplified (no pepper, no rate limiting).

lines.text: When you sign up, a good website never saves your password, so what does it keep instead?
lines.caps: *NEVER SAVES YOUR *PASSWORD | SO WHAT *DOES IT KEEP?

lines.text: Plain text is the worst, because one leak exposes everyone, and encryption is two-way, so attackers can get the original back.
Instead it stores a hash, which is a one-way scramble of your password.
At login, it hashes what you type, and compares the two hashes.
But the same password always gives the same hash, so attackers use lookup tables.
So each user gets a random salt, added before hashing, and identical passwords now look different.
lines.caps: A RANDOM *SALT | ADDED *BEFORE HASHING | NOW THEY *DIFFER

lines.text: But here's the catch: attackers can still guess and compare, so a fast hash helps them, and a slow one like Argon2id hurts them.
lines.caps: BUT THERE IS A *CATCH | *FAST HASH HELPS THEM | *SLOW HURTS THEM

lines.text: So never store the password, store a salted, slow hash, and pick Argon2id.
lines.caps: NEVER STORE THE *PASSWORD | A *SALTED SLOW HASH | PICK *ARGON2ID
